chapters.relation: The editors' introduction argues that dieting — not just food — deserves philosophical attention, and that the Atkins Diet specifically raises 'chewy' questions about how to decide what to eat, what to believe, and whom to believe, precisely because it defies balanced-diet convention and much expert opinion. It opens with Plato's Republic prescription of roasted meats for campaigning guardians (no pots to carry), cites Nietzsche's Ecce Homo and its 'lengthy disquisition' on his own dietary choices as the rare philosophical treatment of diet, and credits Feuerbach with 'Der Mensch ist was er isst' — you are what you eat. It closes by mapping the volume's sixteen essays across Kant, Hume, Nietzsche, Marx, Dewey, environmental and feminist philosophy, critical race theory, and the philosophy of science.

chapters.file: ch10 - The Atkins Diet and Philosophy.md
ch11 - The Atkins Diet and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Auxier, an Atkins dieter, argues the diet works for the reason Dewey gives in Human Nature and Conduct: habits built in calm moments are the bulwark against desire in crisis, and Atkins succeeds by reshaping which gratifications are habitually available — 'a steak for the black eye of desire.' He then transfers Atkins's physiology to thinking: television and advertising serve 'conceptual carbs,' packaged bundles of doubt, emotion, and readiness to act that bypass inquiry and leave the public 'intellectually diabetic' and ideological. Peirce's pragmatic maxim is translated into an eight-step mental exercise (worked through a parent's tattoo-or-piercing doubt about a teenage daughter), while Descartes's hyperbolic doubt is discarded in favor of pragmatism's 'genuine doubt.'

chapters.file: ch12 - The Atkins Diet and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Framed by The Onion's 'New Nietzschian Diet Lets You Eat Whatever You Fear Most' and its 'Fat is dead' riff on the death of God, Irwin argues via Nietzsche's Ecce Homo that 'small things — nutrition, place, climate' matter more than philosophy usually admits, and that dieting belongs to giving style to one's character: we are both artists and works of art, so a 'sound mind in an Atkins body' is self-creation. Drawing on his own two years on the diet (187 to 165 pounds, steadier mood, lower cholesterol), he contends Atkins fits some constitutions — Schwarzenegger's carnivorous persona — and not others: Tony Soprano, devouring gabagool amid agita and fainting spells, could not do Atkins without ceasing to be who he is. Nietzsche's 'One has to know the size of one's stomach' becomes the rule of dietary self-knowledge.

chapters.file: ch13 - The Atkins Diet and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Dennis uses Kant to sort eaters into the fundamentally unfree (Herbert, raised on Atkins and thieving, who merely ploughs on), the fundamentally random (Rita, whose synapses and muscles would fire in chaos), and the autonomous, arguing that only an autonomous person can genuinely decide whether to follow Atkins — by weighing friends' testimonials against the medical establishment rather than habit, whim, or advertising. The categorical imperative grounds the autonomous life: 'lie when you can gain' fails universalization, and treating humanity as an end means offering a vegetarian guest food she is comfortable with instead of pressing Atkins meat on her. His own 'Dan Dennis Diet,' built by experiment and reasoning, illustrates autonomy in practice, and the case of Kitty shows that observing someone's diet never reveals whether its holder is unfree or autonomous.

chapters.file: ch14 - The Atkins Diet and Philosophy.md
ch15 - The Atkins Diet and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Knight places Atkins's caveman utopia — Paleolithic abundance, hunter-gatherer vitality, downfall through agriculture — inside the primitivist tradition running from Ovid's Golden Age to Rousseau's Noble Savage, whose state of nature Rousseau himself admitted was 'mere conditional and hypothetical reasoning' aimed at European corruption. Using postcolonial critics (Spurr, Torgovnick, and Fanon's line that whites who feel 'too mechanized' turn to 'the men of color' for 'human sustenance'), she argues low-carb primitivism is self-reflexive nostalgia — South Beach cannot even date its own paradise — that also freezes living Inuit and Indigenous Australians as Stone Age remnants, hiding the colonial and economic causes of their diabetes and poverty.

chapters.file: ch16 - The Atkins Diet and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: O'Connell extracts Brillat-Savarin's 1825 anti-flour-and-starch regimen — clear soup without croutons, shun beer, rye over white bread — as a 'proto-Atkins' and reconstructs its real argument: farmers fatten livestock on starches, so by Humean 'species of Analogy' starches fatten humans, from which abstinence from floury foods is 'deduced.' Hume's Enquiry Section IX, 'Of the Reason of Animals,' supplies the philosophical audit, distinguishing relations of ideas from matters of fact and grading the animal-to-human analogical inference as probable at best. The chapter ends with Hume's fork turned on the diet-book shelf: any volume without experiential reasoning concerning matter of fact deserves the flames — 'nothing but sophistry and illusion.'

chapters.file: ch17 - The Atkins Diet and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: In an imaginary salon hosted by the baker 'la Brioche,' the goddess Eris drops a golden apple inscribed 'Atkins,' and three philosophers fight over the credit. Rousseau claims Atkins's war on refined flour and 'invented fake food' as his own back-to-nature, state-of-nature legacy; Confucius counters that Americans are 'grazers' without li, that culture is nature's flower, and that only ritual propriety can counteract the advertising that fills the void; Democritus claims the scientific core — 'hyperinsulism,' 'benign dietary ketosis' — as atomism's heir, deriding Rousseau's general will as democratic truth-concocting and Plato's otherworldly philosopher-king. The debate ranges over free will versus scientific prediction-and-control and ends unresolved over a refusal of brioche.

chapters.file: ch18 - The Atkins Diet and Philosophy.md
ch19 - The Atkins Diet and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Steele starts from Orwell's worry that laypeople accept scientific consensus as unreflectively as tribesmen accept witch-doctors — sharpened by Lysenko and Nazi 'racial science' — and answers it with Popper's critical rationalism: since Hume's problem of induction bars proof from instances, we can only provisionally prefer theories that survive severe attempts at falsification, so trusting experts is reasonable exactly when their community tests rather than defends its theories. Kuhn's paradigms explain why dissident alternatives like Atkins talk past the dominant school (Atkins and Agatston are cardiologists, not dieticians), and the 2002–2004 studies showing improved lipids on more fat figure as the kind of surprise that precedes paradigm change. His verdict: neither trusting nor resisting experts is foolish; 'human knowledge is too important to be left to experts.'

chapters.file: ch20 - The Atkins Diet and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Bamford argues that Atkins's insistence that dieters evaluate the plan for their individual needs parallels Nietzsche's cultural therapy: as the death of God left modern culture nihilistic, so a processed-food culture suffers 'nutritional nihilism,' and the 'mega-orthodox' doctors who worship medical consensus with 'religious fervor' treat science as a replacement religion. Reading Ecce Homo's 'question of nutriment' alongside Twilight of the Idols, she shows that Nietzsche's perspectivism — no uninterpreted facts, only interpretations from physiological perspectives — makes each dieter fully responsible for interpretation, which is why Atkins must ask us to think for ourselves. The limit: where Atkins keeps an 'absolute faith in empirical science' (and Atkins Nutritionals mass-markets processed low-carb products), a properly Nietzschean therapy would question that faith too.

chapters.file: ch21 - The Atkins Diet and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Womack tests whether Atkins counts as a Kuhnian paradigm shift, using the Ptolemaic-to-Copernican transition as the model: paradigms define which problems matter, normal science accumulates anomalies, and crisis ends in a new paradigm. Measured against the dieting paradigm's own goals, Atkins flunks — its short-term wins fade by twelve months in the JAMA comparison with the Ornish, Zone, and Weight Watchers diets, with 30–50 percent dropout — so the dieting paradigm itself, which treats obesity as an individual plate problem, is the thing in crisis. Her proposed replacement shifts from the individual to the 'toxic food environment': sidewalks, zoning, food advertising rules, and the French Paradox as the existence proof.

chapters.file: ch22 - The Atkins Diet and Philosophy.md
ch23 - The Atkins Diet and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Bar On examines the Atkins website's country-by-country packaging and asks what kind of commodity the diet is, answering with Marx's Capital: use-value versus exchange-value, money's erasure of qualitative difference (an Atkins cookbook priced like a tub of supplements), and capitalists who produce use-values only as 'material depositories of exchange-value.' Advertising succeeds not by manipulation but because alienated people — labor sold, selves split to fit the job market — already live in exchange relations, and Atkins mediates even the dieter's relation to herself through purchased bars, supplements, and books. Her conclusion: a weight-loss diet only the relatively privileged can afford, in a world where the poor eat carbohydrates because they are cheap, is itself a symptom of the alienation Marx diagnosed.

chapters.file: ch24 - The Atkins Diet and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Wilkerson borrows the social contract tradition — Hobbes's mutual-restraint founding, radicalized by Pateman's sexual contract and Mills's racial contract — to recast antifat bias as a systematic breach of the social contract enforced by medicine (hallway weigh-ins, weight lectures instead of care), employment, transit seating, and TV fat jokes. Against Atkins's medical discourse of the 'obesity epidemic' she assembles Health at Every Size evidence, trans-fat and high-fructose corn syrup data, and the documented health damage of stigma and dieting itself, concluding that Atkins profits from recasting social problems as individual failings. Atkins for Life's success stories (Kerry Feather's volleyball and new husband, Luann Lockhart's proud daughter) are read as testimony that dieting works as ritual self-abasement purchasing group membership — hence Fat Liberation's 'another world is possible.'

chapters.file: ch25 - The Atkins Diet and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Detmer argues moral vegetarianism follows from principles nearly everyone accepts — cruelty, the infliction of unnecessary or disproportionate suffering, is wrong — and that Atkins, which escalates meat eating without being necessary for weight loss, fails both his necessity and proportion tests. Rebutting human superiority, he deploys Rachels's point that no single feature like language is relevant to every difference in treatment and Bentham's 'Can they suffer?', holds factory-farm castration without anesthetic up against the civet-cat musk trade his students already condemn, and answers Narveson's appeal to intuition and the appeal to tradition. Even granting Atkins maximal health benefits, the margin over a well-planned vegetarian diet (Denmark's WWI blockade, the Framingham data) cannot justify the animal suffering, world-hunger, and environmental costs — most of that case drawn from Singer's Animal Liberation.

chapters.file: ch26 - The Atkins Diet and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Cox and Bender subject Atkins to Kant's universal-law formula — could every one of the billion overweight people on earth adopt it? — in a 'factive' thought experiment: a 25 percent rise in animal-protein output, nearly 250 million additional feed-grain acres, overgrazed ranges, and possibly a tenth of the world's remaining forests cleared for pasture. Calling Atkins reductionism's child (a metabolic switch judged on bathroom scales), they use Marx's 'metabolic rift' — soil nutrients shipped to cities, feedlots severing crops from livestock — and the Cartesian body-as-machine (via Federici) to place low-carb's atomized foods (bungalow subs, soy 'mashed potatoes,' pork rinds) as capitalism's latest rupture in the food system. Their verdict: only plant-leaning regimens could survive universalization, and the deeper fix is Wendell Berry's — eating understood as an agricultural act.

chapters.file: ch27 - The Atkins Diet and Philosophy.md
ch28 - The Atkins Diet and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Bentley argues Atkins 'masculinized' dieting: since meat is coded male (the hunter's large game, yang, 'strong as an ox') and dieting female, a diet whose emblematic meal is steak, bacon, and creamed spinach let men come out of the dieting closet — Terry Free's competitive wager, business-school professors trading weight charts, and half-male Atkins success stories against Jenny Craig's sixteen men. The symbolism runs both ways: women now order steak openly, while 'white trash' foods like pork rinds ($840 million in 2003 sales) gained middle-class respectability, a class crossing she explains through Bourdieu's Distinction — taste, habitus, and cultural capital.

chapters.file: ch29 - The Atkins Diet and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Parasecoli reads the Atkins program through Lacanian psychoanalysis: the mirror stage explains why dieters invest in the 'you in the picture' Atkins asks them to visualize — an ideal-ego built from others' gazes and shifting cultural body standards (Botticelli's Venus to Jennifer Lopez); hunger, which Atkins treats as an uncontrollable instinct, occupies the place of the Real that resists symbolization; and 'carbs are bad' functions as the upholstery nail that stabilizes the whole symbolic food system. Science plays the external authority whose impenetrable rationale licenses the dieter's leap of faith, while the body that will not slim on schedule — 'your body is not a machine' — is the Real breaking back in.

chapters.file: ch30 - The Atkins Diet and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: A café dialogue pits second-waver Marie against third-waver Dorothy over whether Atkins can be a feminist tool: Marie wields the feminist critique of Cartesian dualism (Descartes made the mind essential and the body animal, and women were stigmatized as body), Foucault's internalized surveillance — 'every mirror becomes a guard, every scale an alarm,' with Lifetime Maintenance as 'maniacal' hyper-vigilance — Lorde's 'master's tools,' and Young's 'Throwing Like a Girl.' Dorothy answers with Our Bodies, Ourselves self-knowledge, Title IX athletes like Venus and Serena Williams, Frye's Willful Virgin, and existentialist facticity and bad faith (we are in bad faith when we abdicate control), defending dieting as a chosen women's project. The exchange ends drawish, over Brazilian waxes, French women, and whether ugliness is a feminist virtue.

holes.name: Self-Creation (giving style to one's character)
holes.what: Nietzsche's idea (Gay Science 290, developed by Nehamas) that the unity of the self is an achievement, not a given: one molds one's drives, strengths, and even weaknesses into a coherent artistic whole, making life a work of art.
holes.why: Chapter 12's entire case for dieting as the art of living rests on 'giving style to one's character,' and no existing slug covers Nietzschean self-creation.

holes.name: Nihilism
holes.what: Nietzsche's diagnosis that modern culture's values have become devalued and meaningless after the death of God, calling for a therapy of culture rather than new doctrines.
holes.why: Chapter 20 frames Atkins's alternative eating advice as an answer to 'nutritional nihilism' and builds its whole argument on Nietzsche's account of a culture in nihilistic crisis.

holes.name: Metabolic Rift
holes.what: Marx's term (revived by John Bellamy Foster) for the rupture capitalism drives between human production and natural nutrient cycles, e.g. soil fertility shipped to cities and lost as waste.
holes.why: Chapter 26 names Atkins the third metabolic rift — after industrial soil depletion and feedlot agriculture — to argue that atomizing food into nutrients deepens agriculture's break from ecological cycles.

holes.name: Pierre Bourdieu
holes.what: French sociologist-philosopher whose Distinction analyzes how 'taste' and habitus reproduce class distinctions through everyday cultural practices such as food.
holes.why: Chapter 28 uses Bourdieu's habitus and cultural capital to explain how Atkins moved 'white trash' foods like pork rinds into middle-class respectability.

holes.name: Jacques Lacan
holes.what: French psychoanalyst whose mirror stage and registers of the Imaginary, Symbolic, and Real explain how the ego is built from images and language, and what resists symbolization.
holes.why: Chapter 29's entire analysis of Atkins's body imagery, hunger, and carb-phobia is constructed from Lacan's mirror stage, ideal-ego, the Real, and his 'upholstery nails.'
